title: Countryfile star Anita Rani continues to flaunt her London Fashion Week transformation as she makes a chic appearance at Burberry show after THAT daring dress
text:
Countryfile star Anita Rani continued to showcase her glamorous Fashion Week transformation as she attended the star-studded Burberry show on Monday.
Hours after impressing in a daring dress, the presenter, 48, paid homage to the designer with her chic look for the show at 1 Old Billingsgate Walk in London.
Anita opted for a stylish grey trouser suit with one of Burberry's famous scarves draped over her shoulder.
The radio star accessorised her look with a tan leather handbag as she joined stars including Iris Law and Marisa Abela at the show.
Earlier in the day, Anita swapped her comfy Countryfile tweed for a racy dress at the Raw Mango show.
Anita, who has presented the BBC country life show since 2015, added extra height to her frame with pointed patent heels and posed up a storm ahead of taking her seat in the front row.
Countryfile star Anita Rani continued to showcase her glamorous Fashion Week transformation as she attended the star-studded Burberry show on Monday
Hours after impressing in a daring dress, the presenter paid homage to the designer with one of their signature scarves and a grey double-breasted suit for the show
Her appearance comes after she condemned Jacob Elordi for tortured anti-hero Heathcliff in the new Wuthering Heights, because the Australian actor is white.
The Celebrity Race Across The World star claims that Emily Bronte wrote Heathcliff as a non-white character in her 1847 gothic masterpiece.
'At the time, Britain was at the height of the colonial expansion,' says Yorkshire-born Rani. 'This tiny island was getting very rich from doing some very dark things around the world.
'Meanwhile in West Yorkshire, Emily and her two sisters were almost certainly not sitting around crocheting and dreaming of handsome princes.
'They knew all about this because they were educated, they were reading the papers, they were thinking, they were writing and they were raging, and it's in the characters in their books.
'They're women, they are independent, they're clever, they're passionate, they defy convention and they are questioning everything, particularly Victorian morality, which is why it's important that Heathcliff isn't white. It's on the page, and what it does it changes everything. Think about it.'
Heathcliff is described as 'dark-skinned' or 'gypsy in aspect', and as having 'black eyes' by Bronte, who also writes at one point that his 'face is as white as the wall behind him'.
Director Emerald Fennell, who won an Oscar for Promising Young Woman, has stressed that Wuthering Heights is her personal interpretation of how she imagined the novel as a teenager.
Earlier in the day, Anita swapped her comfy Countryfile tweed for a racy dress at the Raw Mango show
The TV host appeared to go braless beneath the daringly plunging cream number which also boasted a black ruffled neckline (Pictured right on Countryfile)
Anita and new boyfriend Alex Lavery made their public debut in September last year during London Fashion Week, where they were spotted beaming at each other.
Anita's new relationship comes two years after she ended her 14-year marriage to technology executive Bhupinder Rehal in September 2023.
A year on, in September 2024, she said that 'life is good' and that she felt like she was entering 'chapter two' of her life.
She told Love Sunday Magazine: 'Life is good, I'm in a good place. I'm focusing on myself and my own wants.
'It's nice to be able to think about the second phase of my life. I've been calling it Chapter Two.'
Anita met her former husband at a rave in east London and married in a Sikh ceremony back in 2009, before splitting last September, believed to be as a result of their hectic schedules.
Anita is dressed in more comfortable attire on the BBC show, which she has hosted since 2015
A source told The Mirror at the time: 'It's really sad but they've decided to separate. Their hectic schedules over the past couple of years have sadly meant they've drifted apart over time'.
Anita admitted she'd found 'freedom' after getting divorced in a candid piece for The Sunday Times, and explained how she has been navigating single life in her forties.
Anita, who was born and raised in Bradford, West Yorkshire by an Indian-born Hindu father and an Indian-born Sikh mother, also revealed how her upbringing had impacted her approach to life.
She confessed that her family believed divorce to be a 'cardinal sin', and while she admitted it 'isn't easy to talk about', she wanted to detail how she feels about her life now so 'that I am answerable to no one'.

title: Moment woman steals £200 of shellfish from Michelin star restaurant as 'langoustine lifter' avoids prison
text:
A woman who was dubbed the 'langoustine lifter' after stealing £200 worth of shellfish from outside a Michelin star restaurant has avoided prison.
Ekaterina Frolova, 46, was convicted last month for the theft and was fined a total of £350.
CCTV posted online last year showed a woman grabbing a box of langoustines that had been delivered and left outside a high-end restaurant called Elystan Street in Chelsea, London.
The footage was shared online by furious chef Phil Howard, who owns the restaurant, after discovering the day's shellfish delivery had vanished.
Calling the person responsible a 'low-life scum bag', he raged on Instagram in November: 'Caught stealing our precious langoustines this morning – you low-life scum bag. Hope you rot in hell with your other hard working mates.'
Restaurant staff said the missing delivery contained around £200 of high-quality langoustines intended for the restaurant's lunch service.
More footage then emerged of similar incidents in the area – including a theft at upmarket florist Petals at Bibendum that is just a short walk from the restaurant.
The Metropolitan Police said today that Frolova, of Lucan Place, pleaded guilty to theft and burglary charges related to both the restaurant and the florist in December last year.
CCTV captured the woman, dressed in jeans and what appear to be slippers, walking up to the front of Elystan Street and stealing a box of langoustines
The missing delivery contained around £200 of high-quality langoustines intended for the restaurant's lunch service
She was remanded in custody and appeared at Westminster Magistrates' court on January 5, where she was fined £350.
As well as the thefts from the florist and the restaurant, Frolova admitted to theft from a pharmacy on Beauchamp Place and another theft from a pharmacy six days later.
Speaking previously, Max Cansdale, who has co-owned Petals at Bibendum for five years, said theft was hitting his business hard.
He said: 'All that can be done for small businesses that face this shoplifting epidemic is to put preventative measures in place.
'All of our products are now secured with fishing wire – so if you pick something up and run off with it...that won't work because you won't be able to tug on it, you'll be stuck and then a staff member will confront you.
'We've got a security guard and at night my team spend a lot more time packing away the whole shop completely away from the gate.
'Even if you had a two-metre broom pushed through the gate, you wouldn't hook anything.
'It's a lot more work for the team. We have team members that come in half an hour earlier to open up, they work later so that they can pack away.'
The footage was posted online by furious chef Phil Howard, who owns the restaurant (pictured), after discovering the day's shellfish delivery had vanished
Elystan Street general manager Becky McLaughlin told the BBC after the theft: 'It’s just somebody that is clearly trying their luck and doesn’t really realise the impact something small to them has on an independent restaurant.
'There is a massive domino effect and it’s a cost that now just has to be swallowed.
'I don't know what they'll do with them but they'll have a very lovely supper,' she said, noting the woman clearly read the label on the box.
'You can tell in the footage that she can see what's written on the box, the contents of what's inside it, and if they were smart then they would know how much it was worth.'
A spokesman for the Metropolitan Police said: 'Ekaterina Frolova of Lucan Place appeared at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Monday, 15 December 2025 where she pleaded guilty to theft and burglary.'
The Met added that she was arrested on 12 December and was remanded in custody.

title: CBS News splashy new hire Peter Attia leaves in disgrace over stomach-churning emails he sent 'friend' Jeffrey Epstein
text:
Acclaimed longevity expert Dr. Peter Attia has stepped down from his new role at CBS News after his close ties to Jeffrey Epstein emerged.
Attia, 52, was with the Tiffany Network for not even a month before his exit on Monday, The Hollywood Reporter revealed.
Epstein's close friendship with Attia was exposed in the latest tranche of emails compiled by feds who investigated the financier and released by Congress.
One disgusting exchange saw Attia use a crude word for female genitalia and tell Epstein that 'it is, indeed, low carb.'
Another from April 2016 saw Attia express his desire to visit  Epstein's notorious private island.
Another from 2015 suggested Attia knew his friendship with Epstein - then already a convicted sex offender - was, at best, ill-advised.
'You [know] the biggest problem with becoming friends with you? The life you lead is so outrageous, and yet I can't tell a soul,' Attia wrote at the time.
In a statement Monday - less than three weeks on from the emails' release -a spokesperson for Attia maintained his 'contributor role was newly established and had not yet meaningfully begun.
Dr. Peter Attia, a well known health influence whose specialty lies in longevity, was with the Tiffany Network for just four weeks before his somewhat abrupt exit on Monday
Jeffrey Epstein's friendship with Attia was exposed in the latest tranche of emails compiled by feds who investigated the financier
'As such, he stepped back to ensure his involvement didn’t become a distraction from the important work being done at CBS. He wishes the network and its leadership well and has no further comment at this time.'
The addition of Attia and other 'new media' contributors to CBS, meanwhile, was touted as a win by Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss on January 27, during an all-hands-on-deck meeting in Manhattan where details were then quickly leaked to the press.
'These individuals are just the start,' Weiss told staffers after showing off a sizzle reel that included Attia and other talents.
'And as you’ve surely seen, they are already in the mix. I urge you to use them more.'
'I’ve talked a little bit about restoring trust and about the kind if journalism that helps us do that. But we also need to do our part to meet audiences where they are and engage them in different ways than before,' the right-leaning editor added at the time.
The decision was met with scrutiny not even a week later, when Attia's name came up multiple times in the documents.
In a statement addressing the mentions, Attia maintained that he met Epstein in 2014 through 'a prominent female healthcare leader' while raising funds for scientific research.
The doctor visited Epstein several times at his New York City townhouse to talk research studies and meet scientists, doctors, business leaders, and even some 'prominent heads of state,' he said.
'[Female genitalia] is, indeed, low carb. Still awaiting results on gluten, though,' one of the emails Attia sent to Epstein read in 2016
Another email suggested Attia knew his friendship with Epstein was controversial
'In retrospect, the presence and credibility of such venerable people in different orbits led me to make assumptions about him that clouded my judgment in ways it shouldn't have,' Attia wrote.
He further claimed that he never treated Epstein, but did own up to answering the sex trafficker more general medical questions and recommending him other doctors.
Attia, in the end, argued that Epstein misled him about the crimes he was convicted of - as many other prominent figures have before him.
Calls for the doctor to resign quickly piled in, after which source who spoke with The Wrap said Weiss was dead-set on keeping Attia over fears she would be seen as weak.
The legacy-media hating journalist has had a tough tenure since taking the reins back in October.
Matt Gutman - a longtime but little-known former ABC journalist who previously worked at the Jerusalem Post - was Weiss's first hire as editor-in-chief. He is now the network's chief reporter.
Executives at ABC let the longtime correspondent go without a fight, a well-placed source told the Daily Mail last month. Others said the move showed Weiss's inexperience.
The rocky start continued with Weiss’s highly publicized town hall with Erika Kirk in December, which proved to be a ratings flop.
Attia's exit comes after months of chaos under new Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss, a former opinion journalist who has never led a major newsroom
Attia was hired by Weiss with 18 other non-typical new media personalites to 'regain trust' with viewers
The elevation of Tony Dokoupil to CBS Evening News from CBS Mornings in January was also widely criticized - with sources who spoke with the Daily Mail calling it a last-ditch move from a leader who is undoubtably desperate.
A few weeks later, Weiss made the decision to pull a 60 Minutes segment set to speak on poor conditions at CECOT (Terrorism Confinement Center) in El Salvador, a prison where the Trump administration has been sending suspected illegal immigrants.
Weiss was appointed by also-new Paramount CEO David Ellison under the pretense of being a disruptor after the company's merger with Skydance.
The Daily Mail has approached CBS News and Paramount for comment.
Weiss, the founder of the Free Press, was paid $150million for the publication in October, by Paramount and CBS.

title: The lies of Britain's last hangman: Albert Pierrepoint boasted about killing 600 people because he wanted to pack out his pub – but the real number was nowhere near
text:
Albert Pierrepoint cut an unlikely figure as a national symbol of death.
A cheerful northern landlord, he liked his beer pulled properly and his pub run without fuss.
To customers drifting into the Help The Poor Struggler near Oldham, he seemed utterly ordinary - polite, dry-witted, with a steady hand on the pump.
Few could imagine that those same hands had ended more lives than anyone else in modern British history.
For more than a quarter of a century, Pierrepoint led an incredible double life - a jovial publican who was also the Home Office’s executioner-in-chief.
Among those he hanged were murderers and traitors, Nazi war criminals, jealous lovers and violent spouses - and in 1955, the last woman ever sent to the gallows in Britain.
He prided himself on speed and composure, claiming he could carry out an execution in just eight seconds, before catching a train home to open up the pub.
However, historians have now raised questions over the extraordinary boasts of Britain's last hangman.
Pierrepoint had claimed to have executed more than 600 people throughout his career, but a study of official records suggests he may have inflated the numbers to 'make out he was more important than he actually was'.
Albert Pierrepoint was a jovial publican who was also the Home Office’s executioner-in-chief - a man who would eventually hang more than 400 people, though he later boasted of a fictitious 600
A notebook owned by Albert Pierrepoint detailing all of the executions he carried out in his 25-year career
On 13 July 1955, Albert Pierrepoint hanged Ruth Ellis (pictured), the glamorous nightclub hostess who shot her lover, racing driver David Blakely. She was 28, blonde, and immediately became a symbol of a nation increasingly uneasy with the death penalty, ending in Pierrepoint's resignation
Pierrepoint publicly insisted that he had no interest in pursuing any kind of macabre record of executions - but in private he would quietly inflate his death toll.
In his 1973 autobiography, Executioner Pierrepoint, he even vowed never to put a number on the executions he carried out.
Yet seventeen years earlier, he had boasted to have hanged more than 600 people - a claim he also repeated to an assistant.
I'm Sam Greenhill, Chief Reporter, and nearly 25 years ago I had an encounter with killer Ian Huntley that still sends shivers down my spine.
Huntley is one Britain’s most notorious child murderers. But when I was invited into his home for tea and biscuits days before he was arrested for the Soham Murders, this was the last thing on my mind. I've written about it in The Crime Desk newsletter - sign up to read it for free.

And in his own diary - a private ledger of death listing the condemned by name, age, height and weight - Pierrepoint arrived at a total of 550 hangings, claiming there to have been 'missing pages'.
But the true figure, painstakingly verified by historian Steve Fielding, author of Pierrepoint: A Family of Executions, is in fact 433.
For a man whose professional reputation rested on exact measurements, this elastic arithmetic seems striking.
Mr Fielding, who also runs The Hangman's Record YouTube channel, told the Daily Mail: 'All hangmen were bound by the Official Secrets Act and I think they believed that the full truth of what they did would never get into the public domain.
'I think Albert was trying to make out he was more important than he actually was, and that no-one would notice if he quietly claimed credit for a few more executions.
'He may have publicly stated that he didn’t want to be seen chasing records, but there was clearly a part of him that wanted to cement his reputation as the definitive hangman.
'The man who had done more than any other.'
This was not the only time Pierrepoint seems to have embellished the truth for some added fame.
After retiring in 1956, he secured a lucrative newspaper deal to reveal the last moments of many of the notorious criminals he executed.
The series, Pierrepoint Speaks - illustrated with photographs of Albert pulling pints behind his bar - enraged the Home Office who threatened legal action.
Only after interviewing witnesses - whose memories clashed with Pierrepoint’s dramatic accounts - did they decide his 'startling revelations' were little more than journalistic embellishment than breaches of state secrets.
Instead pressure was brought to bear on the publishers of Empire News, with the series pulled after two instalments.
Albert Pierrepoint ran the Help The Poor Struggler near Oldham where he seemed utterly ordinary - polite, dry-witted, with a steady hand on the pump
Pierrepoint pictured behind the bar of his Public House in 1955
Seventy years after Pierrepoint quietly resigned from his grim second job - a role paid 'by the neck' - questions also linger over how much he 'enjoyed' his role.
For decades, he insisted he was nothing more than a dutiful civil servant, performing an unpleasant task on behalf of the state.
God-fearing, he claimed he had been chosen to carry out sentences decided by others - taking no pleasure in death, only pride in doing his job efficiently and humanely.
'I was chosen by a higher power for the task which I took up. I was put on this Earth especially to do it...It is something I think should be sacred to me,' he once wrote.
In recent years, historians have begun asking a far darker question: was Albert Pierrepoint really the reluctant executioner he claimed to be - or someone who enjoyed the power and status his role conferred?
An unearthed radio interview aired in 1987, five years before his death, seems to confirm the latter, as he admitted, 'I've enjoyed every bloody minute of it' when asked about state-sanctioned killing.
In 2023, author and historian Ben Macintyre delivered the most incendiary reassessment yet, branding Pierrepoint 'one of Britain’s worst serial killers'.
He wrote: 'More recent research and evidence and changing attitudes towards capital punishment suggest he was something very different.
'A callous, self-important brute, who claimed to be motivated by sacred impulses (as many killers do), fastidiously recorded his trail of death (ditto), relished his own macabre notoriety (ditto), killed several innocent people and went on hanging people, without remorse, long after he had concluded capital punishment was not a deterrent.
'He quit not from moral scruple but over money. He was not mentally ill, like many of his victims, just entirely loathsome.
'In an age of historical mea culpas, the government should consider apologising for Albert Pierrepoint.'
An unearthed radio interview aired in 1987, five years before his death, Albert Pierrepoint (pictured) admitted, 'I've enjoyed every bloody minute of it' when asked about state-sanctioned killing
The gallows at the old Newgate Prison just before it was demolished to build the Central Criminal Court (The Old Bailey) in 1904
To understand the fascinating contradictions at the heart of Albert Pierrepoint, you have to go back to the Pierrepoint family itself, Britain’s execution dynasty.
It began in February 1901, when a 22-year-old Manchester furniture salesman and apprentice butcher sat down to write a speculative letter. Britain’s chief executioner, James Berry, had just been forced out after a series of botched hangings.
'Dear Sir,' wrote Henry Pierrepoint, addressing the Home Secretary directly.
He said he would be 'very thankful' to be considered for the post of public executioner, 'as I have always had a desire for that appointment'.
He listed his height, offered references – and lied about his age to appear more mature.
That brief note set in motion events that would bind the Pierrepoint name to capital punishment for the next half century.
Historian Mr Fielding said Henry spotted an opportunity.
'You have to remember that in 1900, travel itself was a form of excitement,' he said.
'There were no cars, and unless you were on serious business or in the armed forces, most people never went beyond their own county.
'Becoming an executioner meant travelling the country by train, staying in different towns, seeing places most working men would never see.
'People at the turn of the century were also far less squeamish about death. Capital punishment was a fact of life. Mortality was high and the death penalty wasn’t viewed as especially controversial or grotesque.
'If you could stomach it, the job paid extremely well - the equivalent of a month’s wages for a single execution, far more than you’d earn in a factory or shop.'
Henry quickly rose through the Home Office ranks, conducting 105 executions before alcohol destroyed his career. In 1910 he turned up drunk for an execution in Chelmsford and ended up punching his assistant.
His older brother Thomas joined the family business in 1906 after working as a quarryman. The work was relentless. They criss-crossed the country, sometimes carrying out several executions a month.
Thomas later travelled to Ireland in the 1920s as the fledgling state’s official executioner, priding himself on speed. His reputed record from cell to gallows was ten seconds.
He worked into his mid-70s, retiring in 1946 with a final tally just shy of 300.
'Thomas effectively did a full lifetime’s work,' said Mr Fielding. 'Hangmen prided themselves on speed - depending on the proximity of the condemned cell to the gallows, 15 seconds was the average.
'As he aged, his obsession with speed made him hasty and aggressive. One chaplain complained he didn’t have time to put his surplus on before the prisoner was ushered onto the scaffold.
'By 1946, arthritis had set in. He was tolerated during the war because he was reliable and didn’t drink, but retirement was inevitable.'
Albert's father, Henry, and uncle, Thomas, were also executioners, conducting around 400 executions between them
'Table of drops': The workings out of the distance required and the distance to fall for hangman Albert Pierrepoint
Executioners learned to assess bodies quickly, calculate drops precisely and bind limbs efficiently. Too slow or too long, and the result could be horrific.
Henry’s son Albert, who as an 11-year-old imagined death as 'an adventure' and execution as 'romance', excelled under his uncle’s tutelage.
He assisted at his first hanging in 1932 in Dublin - a farm labourer who shot his brother dead in an inheritance feud - followed by a lorry driver who had bludgeoned a domestic servant.
In October 1941, he took the lead for the first time, executing Antonio Mancini at Pentonville prison. Mancini had stabbed to death a rival gangster in a Soho billiard hall.
But it was the Second World War that transformed the youngest Pierrepoint from tradesman to national figure.
In 1945, Britain needed an executioner capable of unprecedented numbers. Dozens of Nazi war criminals were sentenced to death - and Albert was chosen.
Over four years, he executed more than 200 war criminals from Bergen-Belsen and Auschwitz, including Josef Kramer, the 'Beast of Belsen', and Irma Grese, the 21-year-old guard whose cruelty terrified prisoners.
He also pulled the gallows lever on Lord Haw-Haw - fascist William Joyce, the Nazis propaganda voice in Britain.
In the public imagination, Pierrepoint became an avenging angel. One fascist, John Amery, shook his hand and said: 'I’ve always wanted to meet you, Mr Pierrepoint, though not in these circumstances.'
In October 1941, he took the lead for the first time, executing Antonio Mancini at Pentonville prison. Mancini had stabbed to death a rival gangster in a Soho billiard hall
Among Albert's 600 executions was Irma Grese (pictured), the 21-year-old guard whose cruelty terrified prisoners
He also pulled the gallows lever on Lord Haw-Haw - fascist William Joyce, the Nazis propaganda voice in Britain (pictured)
British traitor Joyce (pictured) who broadcast from Nazi Germany as 'Lord Haw-Haw' during WWII is seen in captivity
Another British pro-Nazi adventurer, John Amery (pictured), told Albert ahead of his execution: 'I’ve always wanted to meet you, Mr Pierrepoint, though not in these circumstances.'
Mr Fielding said: 'Just under half of Albert Pierrepoint’s executions were war-related. He hanged 202 people, mostly at Hameln gaol.
'In the public imagination, that transformed him. He became, in many eyes, a kind of public hero for executing Nazis.
'Albert himself said he received a Christmas card every year for several years from a stranger, with £5 enclosed. All the card said was '"Belsen".'
In the early 1950s, Pierrepoint carried out some of Britain’s most controversial executions - cases that would shape public opinion and eventually push the country towards abolition.
One of the those was Timothy Evans, the nervous young Welshman convicted of murdering his wife and baby daughter.
Evans insisted he was innocent. He accused his neighbour, John Christie, of killing them. Pierrepoint hanged him in 1950 with his usual speed. 'I hanged John Christie in less time than it took the ash to fall off a cigar I had left in my room at Pentonville,' he later claimed.
Three years later, Christie was revealed as a serial killer and Evans was found to be innocent.
What became known as the Rillington Place murders was later immortalised in film, with Albert a non-credited adviser.
It is there that we get a fascinating glimpse of Pierrepoint's personality.
Mr Fielding said: 'Albert oversaw the execution scene and some of the secretaries on the set were being sick because he would be so graphic and so light-hearted about it.
'It was quite a serious subject because people believe that Timothy Evans was actually innocent and there's Albert almost making fun of it.'
In the early 1950s, Pierrepoint carried out some of Britain’s most controversial executions - cases that would shape public opinion and eventually push the country towards abolition. One of those was Timothy Evans (pictured)
Evans was convicted of murdering his wife and baby daughter but he accused his neighbour, John Christie, of killing them. Pierrepoint hanged him in 1950 with his usual speed but, three years later, Christie was revealed as a serial killer and Evans was found to be innocent
The iconic actress Diana Dors also found Pierrepoint repugnant, including him in a chapter in her autobiography.
Mr Fielding wrote: 'She recalled her unhappy experiences meeting Albert Pierrepoint, and how during filming a movie, she had been invited back to Help The Poor Struggler with other members of the cast.
'Her reminiscences portrayed the hangman as an attention seeker, who took great pride in his job, and boasted of the people he had hanged.
'She ended the chapter by saying that happily it was the only time she had been in his company.'
Later in 1950, came a work engagement that cut directly into the hangman's life as a landlord.
James Corbitt, a regular in Help The Poor Struggler, murdered his lover in a jealous rage.
He had sang songs with Pierrepoint round the piano and knew exactly what his genial publican did when he wasn’t pulling pints.
In his memoirs, Pierrepoint later reflected on the grim irony of executing a man whom he had known.
'I thought if any man had a deterrent to murder poised before him, it was this troubadour whom I called Tish,' he wrote. 'He was not only aware of the rope, he had the man who handled it beside him singing a duet.'
'The deterrent did not work', he said.
Mr Macintyre claimed in his Times column from 2023 that the execution of Corbitt was an indicator of Pierrepoint's true character. He wrote: 'Britain's most famous hangman was proud of his work but his motives resembled those of the murderers he dispatched.'
Mr Fielding suggests the relationship between Pierrepoint and Corbitt was 'blown way out of context'.
He said: 'Pierrepoint admitted he didn’t know the name of the man he was to hang until he saw him in the condemned cell, which would hardly be the case if they were friends.
'Pierrepoint being a jovial landlord with a good singing voice probably sang duets with lots of customers.'
On 13 July 1955, Albert hanged Ruth Ellis, the glamorous nightclub hostess who shot her lover, racing driver David Blakely.
She was 28, blonde, and immediately became a symbol of a nation increasingly uneasy with the death penalty. He was spat at by crowds as he arrived to perform his duties.
Ruth Ellis (pictured), a Welsh nightclub owner, was the last woman to be hanged for murder in the United Kingdom
Crowds gather outside Wandsworth prison at on the morning of the execution of Ruth Ellis
Albert Pierrepoint was spat at by crowds outside the prison as he arrived to perform his duties.
The Magdala pub in Hampstead where David Blakely was killed by his lover Ruth Ellis, 1955
In February 1956, shortly after Ellis’s execution, Pierrepoint resigned in a row over pay - but while also in talks with the tabloid Empire News for a series of articles 'The Hangman's Own Story'.
He was offered the equivalent of £500,000 today to sensationally reveal the final moments of notorious criminals.
Mr Fielding writes in his book of the first article: 'Illustrated with photographs of Albert playing "find the thimble" with customers, and pulling a pint from behind the bar, the two-page account recounted the tale of his father's first execution and of how Albert himself had first acquired the ambition to follow in the family "business".
'There was nothing to whet the appetite of readers hoping to discover something a little more sensational, graphic or controversial.
'He did, however, propose in future editions to reveal how he hanged Christie ("a coward"), the last moments of Heath, Haigh and Ruth Ellis, and how he went to Germany to hang "The Beasts of Belsen".'
After two instalments, the series collapsed under Home Office pressure. The attorney general wanted to prosecute Pierrepoint for violating the Official Secrets Act.
Eighteen years later, in 1974, Albert resurfaced with a memoir - Executioner Pierrepoint.
The line that dominated the headlines read: 'I do not now believe that any of the executions I carried out acted as a deterrent.'
But Fielding, after years of study, does not accept at face value that Pierrepoint did not believe in the death penalty - but was instead seeking sales.
He said: 'If you've got a book out, and you want to get some headlines in the paper, it's going to get people asking questions, isn't it?
'If he said, "I was a hangman and they all deserved it", it's not got quite the same impact.'
His book also contained glaring inaccuracies and told how he did not want to put a number on his total executions, as to do so would make it sound like he was aiming for a world record.
Mr Fielding said: 'Evidence that Albert certainly had an idiosyncratic sense of humour is not thin on the ground.
'Many people who knew Albert Pierrepoint... have attested that at various times there were signs up over the bar stating 'No hanging around'.
Yet Mr Fielding rejects claims that Pierrepoint was a 'serial killer'.
Albert's death (aged 87), ended the Pierrepoint dynasty - three men who, over 55 years, hanged more than 830 people in eight countries. Pictured: Albert Pierrepoint's execution logbook
He said: 'I find him a very contradictory person. A lot of the things he said in the book weren't actually true.
'He said he never worked with anybody else apart from his uncle, but we know he assisted two other executioners.
'He said he had hanged 600 people, but it's actually 433.
'It's very odd.'
But he added that assertions that Pierrepoint enjoyed killing, or was a serial killer, were 'rubbish'.
He continued: 'He didn't walk around with a black hood on. He was a separate person. He went to the prison, did the job, then went back behind his bar and served his customers.
'It was just a day's work.
'The law needed an executioner, and he was professional enough to do it.
'He detached himself.'
In 1986, Pierrepoint appeared on a BBC talk show. Asked if he had ever hanged the wrong man, he said he slept 'soundly at night' and had merely been a 'servant of the law'.
Aged 87, Albert Pierrepoint died in 1992 in a nursing home in Southport, Merseyside, having spent decades running the Rose and Crown pub in the nearby Lancashire village of Much Hoole.
At that pub in the 1950s, coach parties would stop off with customers obtaining autographs from Pierrepoint.
Mr Fielding said: 'He ultimately was very media savvy because he knew it was good for business.
'Your execution would be on the front page of the newspapers and suddenly, your pub's full and your till's bursting.'
With him ended the Pierrepoint dynasty - three men who, over 55 years, hanged more than 830 people in eight countries.
Capital punishment was eventually abolished in Britain in 1969.

title: Kate Ferdinand dedicates sweet message to her husband Rio as she thanks him for 'loving her as she is' after admitting she's struggling with family move to Dubai
text:
Kate Ferdinand has dedicated a sweet message to her husband Rio as she thanked him for 'loving her as she is' with an album of snaps shared to Instagram on Monday.
The former TOWIE star, 34, has been open about struggling with relocating to the UAE after she moved with Rio, 47, his daughter Tia, 14, their son Cree, four, and two-year-old daughter Shae in August last year.
But in recent posts about her healthy lifestyle, Kate has appeared to have become more settled in her new daily routine with Rio.
In one snap, Kate can be seen eating an array of healthy fruits and drinking green smoothies.
While in another, she shared a sweet picture of movie night in bed after being gifted a large pink and red bouquet.
Alongside her post, she penned: 'My love ❤️ I’m not sure what I would do without you.
Kate Ferdinand has dedicated a sweet message to her husband Rio as she thanked him for 'loving her as she is' with an album of snaps shared to Instagram on Monday
The former TOWIE star has been open about struggling with relocating to the UAE after she moved with Rio his daughter Tia, 14, their son Cree, four, and daughter Shae, two, last year
'Thank you for loving me just as I am. A weekend of lazy mornings, long walks & movie nights with you'.
Kate recently admitted she had been struggling with their move to Dubai and broke down in tears as she admitted she's 'missing her family'.
She confessed while Dubai has been an 'amazing' place to live, she's 'struggled' with being apart from Rio's two eldest sons Lorenz, 19, and Tate, 17, who have stayed in the UK for their football careers.
Opening up about their decision to move in March's edition of Men’s Health UK, Rio said: 'I look at it like an adventure. My life has been governed by the fixture list while playing football and then, post-career, being a pundit.
'There aren't many opportunities in life where you get time to make a big change, have an adventure, step out of your comfort zone and explore something new. So this is it. This is what we wanted to do.'
Kate admitted to Women’s Health UK that she's very in touch with what works well for her mental health, declaring exercise and therapy helps if she is 'struggling'.

In one snap, Kate can be seen eating an array of healthy fruits and drinking green smoothies
While in another, she shared a sweet picture of movie night in bed after being gifted a large pink and red bouquet
Alongside her post, she penned: 'My love ❤️ I’m not sure what I would do without you. Thank you for loving me just as I am. A weekend of lazy mornings, long walks & movie nights with you'
Kate recently admitted she had been struggling with their move to Dubai and broke down in tears as she admitted she's 'missing her family'
She explained: 'I want to look good and I'm happier when I look good, I have to be honest. But I would always choose to exercise because I work out for my mental health, too.
'I also want to be a healthy role model for my children: they see me working hard in the gym and that makes a difference...
'I'm quite aware of how I feel and what I need to do in order to make myself feel better. If I need help, I'll have therapy. If I'm struggling, I'll go outside and go for a walk, I'll talk to people.'
Speaking about her struggle with the move last month, she said: 'I feel like we've opened our eyes to a different world. But I love London, I love the UK. I love so many things about the UK.
'I do feel happy in Dubai, but I'm just missing a part of me.'
Kate added that the move has also helped Rio be more 'present' with his family, after he stepped back from his role as a pundit for TNT Sports last year.
She added: 'I think it's an amazing place to live, I think it's amazing for the children. The children are thriving and happy and living a life of just outside freedom.
'Rio loves it so much. I am enjoying it, but I miss home quite a lot. I get upset. I miss the big boys a lot and I'm just struggling with that.
'I know this decision is right for my younger children and as a family we are settled there, but the boys are following their football careers. So they're doing what they want to do otherwise they'd be with us.
'But it's very hard because we've been through so much as a family and we've always been together and that's a huge adjustment.'

title: YouTuber 'stabbed pregnant girlfriend to death while staging fake live stream in bid to cover his tracks', court told
text:
A YouTuber accused of stabbing his pregnant girlfriend to death 'put on an act' to cover his tracks - including a fake live stream, a court was told.
Natalie McNally, 32, was 15 weeks pregnant when she was killed in her home in Lurgan, Northern Ireland, a week before Christmas in 2022.
Stephen McCullagh, 36, from Woodland Gardens, Lisburn, has denied her murder, but the court was told he 'put on an act' to cover his tracks.
The court heard this included a tearful 999 call to police, faking a six-hour video game live stream and suggesting that an ex-partner of Ms McNally's had been responsible, telling police 'someone had knocked 10 bells out of her'.
As the trial at Belfast Crown Court got underway on Monday morning, McCullagh sat in the dock while Ms McNally's loved ones watched on from the public gallery.
Setting out the case against McCullagh on Monday morning, prosecuting barrister Charles MacCreanor KC described a murder that was 'planned, calculated and premeditated, one which he (McCullagh) hoped to get away with'.
He described how in the days after the murder, McCullagh had left his phone at Ms McNally's family home while it was recording, telling the jury it is up to them to decide whether that had been deliberate.
Ms McNally's cause of death was found to have involved compression of her neck, 'suggestive of finger tips grasping', Mr MacCreanor said.
YouTuber Stephen McCullagh, 36, of Woodland Gardens, Lisburn, has denied the murder of Natalie McNally, but, court was told he 'put on an act' to cover his tracks
Natalie McNally, 32, was 15 weeks' pregnant when she was killed in her home in Lurgan a week before Christmas in 2022
She also suffered three stab wounds to her neck caused by a bladed weapon and five lacerations to the back, top and right of her head 'in keeping with having sustained at least five heavy blows'.
Mr MacCreanor said any of these could have caused death alone.
He continued: 'Natalie McNally was pregnant at the time and Stephen McCullagh was the father of her unborn child.'
Her time of death has been estimated to be between 8.50pm and 9.30pm on Sunday December 18, 2022.
Mr MacCreanor said McCullagh, known on YouTube as Votesaxon07, concocted a 'cover story' that he had been livestreaming himself playing video games on the evening of Sunday December 18.
Prosecution argue that McCullagh had pre-recorded six hours of himself playing video games which he broadcast as live that Sunday evening and took a bus to Ms McNally's home in Lurgan and murdered her.
CCTV footage and clips from inside the bus were played. They showed a man wearing a beanie-style hat with a 'mop of black hair' underneath and his face mostly covered.
The man is seen getting on a bus in Dunmurray and getting off in Lurgan before walking towards Ms McNally's house.
The prosecution claims he may have changed his clothes and got a taxi back to his home in Lisburn, with footage also shown of a taxi, and a figure getting into it and being left in the 'area just outside McCullagh's house in Lisburn' around 11pm.
An examination of McCullagh's devices by police showed he had searched for bus times to Lurgan and that he had unlocked his phone a few minutes after the taxi moved off.
Mr MacCreanor suggested the 'mop of black hair' bore a comparison with a wig which McCullagh had posted a picture of himself wearing as part of a dress-up costume on Instagram previously.
Put to McCullagh during police interview, the court heard he responded saying: 'It seems that the suspect did take a taxi to my house, I have no idea who this person was, but I think that is it obvious that the true killer of Natalie has left a clear circumstantial trail to link me to the murder.
Noel and Bernie McNally, parents of Natalie McNally, outside Belfast Crown Court today ahead of a trial for Stephen McCullagh
Natalie McNally's brother Brendan (second left) and family members outside Belfast High Court
'I have no idea where they went after they entered my property, but they could easily have jumped the fence and made their way without being seen.'
McCullagh's distressed-sounding 999 call on the night of Monday December 19 was also played during the first day of the trial.
The court heard he told police the last time he saw Ms McNally had been on Sunday afternoon.
'On the prosecution case, this call is false, it's an act, it's put on by him, part of his plan to do the murder and get away with it,' Mr MacCreanor KC said.
The ambulance service and police were quickly at the scene and reported finding McCullagh with Ms McNally, he said.
He said: 'Natalie McNally is lying at the top of the stairs... which was the living area of the home.
'It's clearly apparent to paramedics that Natalie McNally is dead, everything is consistent with this being an attack upon her, presence of blood and the visible injuries.
'Stephen McCullagh is described by the paramedics as performing CPR to the female and he's described as being quite visibly upset.'
He said police described McCullagh as being 'distraught and overcome'.
'Again, we say this is all part of an act, a front,' he said.
During the 999 call, McCullagh is heard audibly upset and sobbing as he asked for emergency services to come to Ms McNally's address in Lurgan, urging: 'Please come as soon as you can.'
The operator talks McCullagh through how to position Ms McNally and administer CPR compressions as he waited for paramedics to arrive, encouraging him to 'keep going', telling him he was giving her the best chance.
Paramedic Graham Thompson, who said he had been the first into Ms McNally's house after the 999 call, was the first witness to give evidence.
He said he saw a very pale female lying on the floor at the top of the stairs and 'a lot of blood had been lost', adding her hands and lips were purple/blue.
He also said a 'visibly upset' gentleman was on his knees performing CPR and had had to tell him to stop, and there was no hope of resuscitation at that stage.
Constable Archibald described arriving at the house to find the front door open and noticing 'quite a strong foul smell'.
She said she took a visibly distraught and crying McCullagh to the police car to talk to him and to both allow him privacy and the emergency services space to work.
'I had a gentleman who was visibly distraught, very upset, who had just witnessed something very traumatic, so my initial response at that point was to console him as best as I could,' she said.
She said during their conversation he said he did not really speak to his family, but wanted to speak to a friend for support.
'He kept saying 'Why? Why my Natalie, why my Natalie, and who would do such a thing', and I do remember thinking that seems a bit odd because at this point it wasn't confirmed to being treated as a murder or even as suspicious at this point,' she told the court.
The final witness, another first responder, Constable Feeley told the court he saw a knife around three or four feet behind Ms McNally's body.
He said he saw 'a large amount of blood' surrounding Ms McNally, on the walls and into the living room.
He also described seeing McCullagh, and described him as 'distraught, overcome with grief, crying and nearly falling about the place'.
The trial continues.

title: Declassified CIA files reveal chilling blueprint to manipulate Americans' minds through covert drugging with vaccines
text:
A newly released CIA document reveals a chilling blueprint to manipulate minds through covert drugging experiments.
The report, added to the CIA's reading room in 2025, details the government's once top-secret Project Artichoke that ran from 1951 to 1956, focusing on behavior control, interrogation techniques and psychological manipulation.
The seven-page document, titled 'Special Research for Artichoke,' with an attachment labeled 'Suggested Fields for Special Research Relative Artichoke,' outlines proposals to develop chemicals capable of altering human behavior.
It discusses drugs designed for both immediate effects, like truth serums and long-term influence, potentially administered through food, water, alcohol or cigarettes.
Researchers also suggested that such substances could be disguised in medical treatments such as vaccinations or injections.
The CIA was also looking into methods beyond chemicals, listing hypnosis, sensory deprivation, gases and other psychological methods for interrogation and behavioral control.
Artichoke served as a precursor to the CIA's MKUltra program, which later broadened mind-altering experiments on a larger scale.
Many files were destroyed in the 1970s, leaving the full extent of the research and how far it progressed unknown.
The report, added to the CIA's reading room in 2025, details the government's once top-secret Project Artichoke that ran from 1951 to 1956, focusing on behavior control, interrogation techniques and psychological manipulation
The document was declassified in 1983, but has resurfaced on social media, where users are shocked to see the CIA discussing methods for 'drugging entire populations.'
Project Artichoke emerged during the early Cold War, a period marked by intense anxiety over communist powers and reports of brainwashing techniques used on American prisoners of war in Korea.
Internal CIA memos suggested that US intelligence feared enemy nations had developed ways to control human thought and behavior, prompting the agency to explore its own capabilities.
The declassified document reveals the depth of this research, noting the need for a study 'to determine what drugs are best suited for direct use on subjects along the lines of amytal and pentothal and which drugs are best for an indirect or long-range approach to subjects.'
The researchers involved in the secret program emphasized that long-term compounds should be capable of producing 'an agitating effect (producing anxiety, nervousness, tension, etc.) or a depressing effect (creating a feeling of despondency, hopelessness, lethargy, etc.).'
They also outlined practical considerations for concealment, such as substances that could be introduced surreptitiously in 'food, water, Coca-Cola, beer, liquor, cigarettes, etc.,' highlighting the CIA's focus on undetectable methods of influence.
Moreover, the report recommended consulting with the Army Chemical Warfare Service, noting they have conducted 'exhaustive studies along these lines' that could provide specific guidance for the program.
Beyond drugs, Artichoke explored a wide range of psychological tools.
The CIA files discuss drugs designed for both immediate effects, like truth serums and long-term influence, potentially administered through food, water, alcohol or cigarettes (STOCK)
Sections of the document discussed 'hypnosis,' 'psychological techniques' and 'gases, aerosols, and oxygen deficiencies,' demonstrating that the CIA sought to combine chemical, environmental and mental approaches.
Researchers questioned whether such methods could compel individuals to perform actions against their own will, including potentially criminal acts, without leaving conscious awareness of their behavior.
Human experimentation under Artichoke often involved vulnerable subjects, including prisoners, military personnel and psychiatric patients, typically without informed consent.
While much of the documentation was destroyed in 1973, remaining files suggested that the CIA and its collaborators systematically explored the limits of psychological manipulation, with ethical considerations frequently subordinated to perceived national security needs.
Artichoke evolved into the more expansive MKUltra program in 1953, which pushed experimentation further, particularly with hallucinogens like LSD.
MKUltra involved hundreds of subprojects at universities, hospitals, and prisons, many of which used unwitting subjects, drawing outrage when the programs were exposed in the 1970s by congressional hearings, including the Church Committee.
Gangster James 'Whitey' Bulger, a former organized crime boss, was used as a test subject in 1957 while an inmate at the Atlanta penitentiary.
He explained he was one of eight convicts in a panic and paranoid state while in MKUltra.
'Total loss of appetite. Hallucinating. The room would change shape. Hours of paranoia and feeling violent,' Bulger penned.
'We experienced horrible periods of living nightmares and even blood coming out of the walls. Guys are turning into skeletons in front of me. I saw a camera change into the head of a dog. I felt like I was going insane.'

title: Mother-of-three Ann Heron was sunbathing in her garden when she was stabbed to death by a mystery attacker… 35 years later her killer has never been found but police only have ONE suspect
text:
Ann Heron never missed an opportunity to sunbathe and the garden of her quaint country home in Middleton St George, just outside Darlington, was the perfect place to relax.
But as Ann, 44, soaked up the rays, her mind perhaps drifting to a night out with friends later that evening, she had no idea of the horror that lay in wait.
The tranquillity of her afternoon on the hottest day of the year was about to be shattered in the most barbaric of ways.
Preyed upon without warning, Ann was viciously attacked on her front lawn and carried into her home.
The glamorous mother-of-three was found by her husband Peter with her throat slit and lying in a pool of blood in their living room, her bikini bottoms removed.
Peter is the only person who has ever been charged with Ann's murder. And although charges were dropped due to a lack of evidence, police say he remains a suspect to this day.
Ann's case remains unsolved nearly thirty six years after the horrifying attack on August 3 1990. Her family has been forced to live in agony ever since.
The case has baffled detectives with seemingly no motive, no murder weapon and nothing to suggest she had any enemies.
As the hunt for Ann's killer goes on, her son Ralph Cockburn - a retired murder detective – tells the Daily Mail: 'The big question for me is not who, it's why.
'I've thought about the motives, could it just have been someone randomly passing by, could it have been someone attempting a sexual assault? The list is endless, but I just can't comprehend why.'
Murder victim Ann Heron, whose body was found at her home near Darlington on August 3 1990
Ann's son Ralph Cockburn - a retired murder detective - sat down with an interview with the Daily Mail. He holds a framed picture of his mother
Aeolian House, where Ann Heron was murdered. She was sunbathing out the front when she was attacked
To the casual observer, Ann and Peter Heron seemed to have it all.
A pretty detached house, a loving family, and a comfortable life thanks to Peter's job as an executive at a local haulage firm.
The couple met in 1979 when Ann moved to the Isle of Bute with her first husband and their three children.
Peter was on a golfing trip and after a chance encounter the couple fell in love.
Both were stuck in unhappy marriages and each had three children. But Ann made the decision to leave her family behind in Scotland to move in with Peter and his daughters in 1982.
She introduced her new partner to her two sons and daughter at her mother's house in Bute and told them about her plans.
Ralph recalls: 'I was a 16-year-old boy, I probably didn't say the nicest things. I didn't speak to Peter for a couple of months... but I accepted that's who she wanted to be with.'
When Ann moved down to Darlington, Ralph, his sister Ann-Marie and their brother - then 16, 15 and six - moved back to Glasgow with their father, also a policeman.
Ralph would go and visit his mother, but Ann-Marie later moved in with her.
Ann and Peter tied the knot in 1986, but shortly before her death she made contact with her ex-husband, Ralph's father, in which she spoke of her desire to return to Scotland.
Ann-Marie previously told how her mother dearly missed her family and had a 'sadness in her eyes' the last time she saw her.
I'm Sam Greenhill, Chief Reporter, and nearly 25 years ago I had an encounter with killer Ian Huntley that still sends shivers down my spine.
Huntley is one Britain’s most notorious child murderers. But when I was invited into his home for tea and biscuits days before he was arrested for the Soham Murders, this was the last thing on my mind. I've written about it in The Crime Desk newsletter - sign up to read it for free.

Advertisement
While, unknown to his wife, Peter had embarked on an affair with a barmaid at a local pub, a relationship that would not be revealed until after her murder.
In fact, on the day of Ann's murder, he had even driven a longer route back from a meeting to try and catch her on a dog walk less than two hours before he found his wife dead.
Peter and Ann's emotional turmoil is in stark contrast to the scenes of domestic bliss played out on the day of her murder.
Ann - a part-time carer - had spent the morning in Darlington with her friend Dawn, enjoying a portion of chips at McDonalds and picking up a gift for an 18th birthday party she was looking forward to that evening.
At around 1pm, she returned to the rural four-bedroom detached home.
As he did everyday at lunch, Peter left work in Darlington and made the short five-minute drive back home to meet Ann.
The couple ate and caught up in their sprawling garden, unaware that these would be the last words they would ever utter to one another.
When Peter returned to the office at 2pm, 'sunworshipper' Ann cleared away their plates and began to sneak in a few more hours in the sun before her night out.
Unusually, she sat outside the front of the house as a farmer who was harvesting had kicked up a cloud of dust at the back.
Ann took a phone call at about 2.30pm from her best friend, Sheila Eagles, in which they discussed sharing lifts for the party that night.
She was then spotted sunbathing by a friend passing by her garden on a bus around an hour later.
But when Peter returned home from work just before 6pm, instead of finding her getting ready, he walked into a scene from a horror film.
Ann had been savagely attacked as she sunbathed. As her feet were clean, it is believed her killer then carried her inside, stabbed her in the neck and left her lifeless body on the floor of the living room.
Her bikini bottoms had been removed but police said there were no signs of sexual violence.
A radio remained switched on, her books and cigarettes were found nearby and the family border collie was waiting outside.
No one was ever arrested over Ann's death until 2005 when Peter was charged after new technology allowed for further DNA testing to take place and his semen was found in his wife's throat.
However, the case was dropped after just 12 weeks due to a lack of evidence and his family have been fighting to clear his name ever since, arguing that it is completely reasonable that his DNA was found on his wife in their home.
Peter has always denied murdering his ex-wife.
Peter Heron (pictured) was charged with murdering his wife 15 years after her death. The charges were later dropped due to a lack of evidence
Aeolian House pictured today. Ann was lying at the front of the house as is pictured here
Ralph Cockburn is pictured with his mother, Ann Heron, at his police passing out parade in 1983
A picture of Ann Heron with Ralph and his son, her grandson, in 1990 - the same year she tragically died
By 1990, Ralph was working his dream job as a murder detective in Scotland's Criminal Investigation Department (CID).
In May that year, he was investigating the murder of an 11-year-old girl, Christine Lee, and the killer was arrested using DNA evidence, then in its early stages.
Having worked brutal 12 hours shifts for weeks, he decided to go and visit his mother in Darlington with his son and wife, who was heavily pregnant with a second child. Ann would never meet her new grandchild, who was born a month after her murder.
Ralph recalls telling his mother and his stepfather Peter about how he and his homicide squad had snared Christine's killer using DNA.
'I still remember to this day Peter Heron turning around and saying to me, 'So, how does somebody get away with murder if you've got this DNA now?' Ralph says.
'It doesn't mean he's involved. It probably was just a flippant comment and a question that anybody would ask. But you still keep going back to that.'
While the killer's identity is unknown, Ann's son insists the only person he can rule out is himself and anyone is 'fair game'.
During the first week after the murder, Ralph drove down to Darlington to speak to the police before returning to his house, near Loch Lomond.
'Two or three days later, Peter Heron said he wanted to come up and see us,' Ralph says. 'He came up with his daughter, Debbie, at the house in Loch Lomond.
'At that point, I thought he must been a terrible state and he walked in with Debbie and very, very quickly I thought there's not a good feeling here. He was a mess, but there was just something that I couldn't put my finger on and still can't put my finger on.
'About a week later, we then heard through the press that he had been having an affair with the barmaid at a local golf club.
'He had actually introduced me to her when he took me for a pint to the golf club.'
Ralph and Peter have not spoken since he visited Loch Lomond in 1990.
'From that point on, he's just refused to speak to me,' Ralph says, speculating that it could be down to his shame from the affair.
The Durham police investigation involved 65,000 man-hours, 4,500 statements and 4,061 interviews in the early stages.
Although the investigation has been active for 35 years, the police force reinvigorated their inquiries in January 2022 after a meeting with Ann's family.
Police analysts are now re-examining forensics using modern techniques as well as reviewing Peter's movements and drawing together a comprehensive timeline.
One theory is that the killer parked in a layby and was watching Ann sunbathe before pouncing.
A blue car was central to the investigation since two witnesses had seen it near the Herons' home.
One saw the vehicle outside the house at about 4.45pm while another saw it driving at speed down the drive at around 5.05pm.
The driver was described as being a sun-tanned man, aged 35 to 45. But neither the driver nor the vehicle has ever been found.
In October 1994, someone started sending confession letters to the Northern Echo newspaper, Durham Constabulary and Mr Heron.
In one to the editor of the local newspaper, they boasted about the killing, beginning with: 'Hello editor, it's me... Ann Heron's Killer!' and signed it off 'The Killer'.
The letters contained sick details about the murder, but to this day it is not known whether it was simply a hoax or the genuine killer.
Pictured is the drive up to Aeolian House. The property is now a kennels
Ann Heron is pictured with her mother, Ralph and Ralph's son
Ann Heron is pictured on her wedding day. She would later go onto marry Peter Heron and move to Darlington
Jen Jarvie, a private investigator from Detective Rooms, is adamant that Peter's name has been unfairly blackened.
The prime suspect, as far as Ms Jarvie is concerned, is Michael Benson, a career criminal who had absconded from jail in 1989, had an aunt in nearby Eaglescliffe and owned a blue car.
Benson, who had been convicted of firearms and theft offences, was ruled out as a suspect by police who claimed he was out of the country at the time of the murder. He died in 2011.
Ms Jarvie, who started investigating Ann's case in 2015, said: 'In 1990, Benson was on the run and he had relatives in Eaglescliffe, which is just a couple of miles away from the murder side.
'He travelled extensively. He fits the profile of somebody who would do this. He fits the description. He had the propensity for violence and I have a psychiatric report which indicated that he has the kind of psychological makeup that could actually do this.'
A Crimewatch appeal was released in October 1990, featuring a reconstruction of Ann's horrific murder.
A month later, Hampshire Police also featured a Crimewatch appeal about the whereabouts of Benson, describing how he fled prison while on day release in May 1989. He got married that summer, but left his wife in May 1990 and disappeared, taking her dark blue metallic Ford Orion.
Ms Jarvie believes police have ruled Benson out because 'they still believe that Peter is a suspect'.
'I've been able to prove that Peter has an alibi from 2pm until 6pm, when he discovers Ann, and if they would ever consider another suspect, then they would have to say that Peter was innocent which they they won't do.
'This is a nearly 91-year-old man whose reputation for the past 30 years has been tarnished.'
Ms Jarvie says she is frustrated by the police's claim that there are two hours of Peter's afternoon unaccounted for.
Ms Jarvie claims that Peter returned to his workplace, Stiller, after finishing lunch with Ann at 2pm. He is then said to have remained in the office until he received a call at 3.15pm from his clients at Cleveland Bridge, an engineering firm just down the road.
At 3.45pm, Peter left Stiller for an impromptu meeting with three clients who stated he was there and that he left at 4.20pm.
Instead of making the short five-minute journey back to his office, Peter then took a longer 22-minute drive via Neasham.
Ms Jarvie says he did this because he wanted to drive past his barmaid mistress who walked her dog at the same place every day.
Peter wanted to give her a wave but he never saw her.
However, the private detective says that he was seen making this journey by various people, including an off-duty police officer.
He returned to the Stiller office at 4.45pm, speaking to owner Paul Stiller about his new Mercedes in the car park, Ms Jarvie says.
Pictured is Ann and her ex-husband. She had been in contact with him to say she wanted to return to Scotland before her death
Ms Jarvie adds: 'After 5pm, he goes into the office and that's where he stays until he leaves at about 5.45pm to go home.
'He's wearing the same clothes all day, which is a light pair of trousers and a light shirt and obviously gets home and discovers this absolutely horrific scene.'
Ms Jarvie says she is one of few people to have seen the crime scene photos, explaining: 'There was a substantial amount of blood loss because of the horrific injuries that were inflicted on Ann's throat.
'Anybody who committed that heinous crime would have been covered in blood and Peter was wearing the cream pair of trousers and a cream shirt, the same items that he'd worn all day.'
Two years after Ann's death, Peter began a new relationship with mother-of-two Freda Buddie. She helped him to cope with the tragedy and moved into Aeolian House with him. Freda, who battled with cancer, passed away in 2005.
Ms Jarvie and Ann's family are determined to find the killer after 35 years and hope advancements in DNA can help them.
The idea of his mother's murder being unsolved is something that has haunted Ralph - who was 26 when his mother died - and ultimately led him to retiring from the police.
He said: 'The frustration is that nobody has ever been caught. There have been lots of people of interest, lots of suspects. They've still got DNA and samples that they can test.
'I'm forever hopeful that one day I'm going to get a knock on the door.
'Somebody somewhere must know because the person who's done it has not gone for this amount of time without somebody knowing something.'
Ralph - who has three children from his first marriage and another two stepchildren with his second wife of 17 years Denise - feels heartbroken that his mother has 'missed out' on special moments with grandchildren.
But he defiantly says: 'I have tried to turn what happened to my mum into a positive and that has changed my life.
'She only had 44 years on this planet so reaching the age of 44 was a big milestone for me.
'That was me now living longer than she lived. From that point on, I've said to myself I'm living for her now as well.'
Jen Jarvie's prime suspect is Michael Benson (pictured), a career criminal who had escaped jail, had an aunt in nearby Eaglescliffe and owned a blue car
This is a copy of the letter sent by the alleged killer of Ann Heron to the editor of the Northern Echo in 1994. It is not known if this was sent by the genuine killer.
Events were reconstructed for BBC's Crimewatch UK in October 1990, including the blue car (pictured) seen speeding away from Ann Heron's house
A family photo of Ann Heron, her parents and siblings
To this day, no one has ever discovered why Ann - an innocent mother-of-three - was targeted.
She simply lay outside to bask in the August sunshine during what was a blissful heatwave summer in Britain.
Many flocked to beaches and parks, but Ann had the luxury of relaxing in the safe space she called home.
But on August 3 1990, an intruder made their way into the grounds of her country home and snatched her life away in a split-second.
Her murderer, meanwhile, is still at large, living a life of freedom while inflicting decades of grief and trauma on Ann's loved ones.
Detective Superintendent Craig Rudd, of Durham Constabulary said: 'It is now 35 years since Ann was tragically found dead in her own home in Darlington.
'Our Major Crime Team continues to review the case and investigate any new information in the hope of identifying evidence to prove who is responsible.
'We would urge anyone who might know something from that day, however insignificant they think it might be to come forward and get in touch. It is never too late.
'Ann's family have been left devastated by what happened – they deserve closure, and we will never give up trying to find who killed her.
'Information can be reported to Durham Constabulary via 101 or anonymously via Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.'
A spokesman added: 'Peter Heron was designated as a suspect for the murder of Ann Heron in 2005, this status has not changed.'
The force said it has 'undertaken considerable investigation' into Benson but concluded there is no evidence to place him in the area at the time of Ann's murder. They believe he was abroad.

title: Trump wildly sidetracks during event with angel families as he reveals he paid for victim's mother to 'get her eyes fixed'
text:
Donald Trump dramatically paused solemn remarks at the White House with an unusual comment.
The president was honoring the families of victims killed at the hands of illegal immigrants, including 22-year-old nursing student Laken Riley and others.
But he abruptly changed course when he spotted one of the angel family mothers in the crowd wearing glasses.
It was Patty Morin, the mother of Rachel Morin, 37, who was raped and murdered by El Salvadoran illegal immigrant Victor Martinez-Hernandez, 24, while she was hiking in Bel Air, Maryland in 2023.
'Are your eyes OK?' Trump questioned as he looked at the crowd of angel families gathered at the White House on Monday.
'I gave her money to get her eyes fixed. A lot of money to get her eyes fixed,' Trump explained to those who didn't already know. 'That doctor ripped me off, but that's OK.'
Morin said that she was having surgery on Wednesday.
'Well, you get them done,' Trump instructed. 'She's almost blind – cataracts.'
Donald Trump interrupted his own remarks during an event with angel families on Monday, February 23, 2026 to have a conversation with one mother who he said he gave money for a cataracts correction operation
Trump said that gave Patty Morin (pictured), the mother of a woman killed by an illegal immigrant, money to get eye surgery
'I hope you have a good doctor. He's an expensive doctor, top of the line,' he added, saying he was surprised she was still wearing glasses after he gave her money for the surgery.
It came after Trump stopped himself from continuing to talk about how New York City volunteer snow-shovelers needed government ID as he complained that the state doesn't require voters to do the same.
'It's so crazy, you know the mayor of New York – and he's a very nice person, I met him – but his ideology's not too good. But we're having a massive snow storm right now. And I've heard that he's asked people to come out and shovel the snow,' Trump rambled.
'Ok, so you get a shovel and you start shoveling, right? What the hell, you're not going to help too much, but you can help and – hello darling, how are you?' he said, abruptly interrupted his tangent.
'No, right behind you. Look, my friend, right? Are you OK? Yes, you. Are you OK?' he said beginning an exchange with Morin.
It wasn't the only time his remarks went off topic.
The president also compared himself to those he says are the most consequential presidents, including John F. Kennedy and Abraham Lincoln, both of whom were assassinated.
Trump welcomed angel families onto the stage as a he signed the National Angel Family Day Proclamation
'They only go after consequential [presidents],' Trump realized. 'So maybe I want to be a little bit less consequential. Can we hold it back a little bit?'
'Let's be a normal president for a little while,' he added.
Later in his remarks at the White House on Monday, Trump said: 'I don't know how long I'll be around. Got a lot of people gunning for me, don't I?'
It comes after an armed man was shot and killed by authorities when he raised a shotgun after breaching the security perimeter at Trump's Mar-a-Lago club over the weekend.
Trump was not in Florida at the time of the incident and was instead spending a rare weekend in Washington, DC.

title: Rapper Luci4 dead at age 23: Cause of death unknown but grandparents are 'suspicious' of his passing
text:
Rapper Luci4 has passed away at age 23.
A trailblazer in a niche genre of trap music called sigilkore, Luci4 - born James Dear - is behind the songs BodyPartz, All Eyez on Me, Ave Domina Lilith, and more.
His death was confirmed by his manager, Kayla G, who announced her client had died on Sunday, February 22.
The L.A. County Medical Examiner notes Luci4 passed at a private residence and with the cause of death being deferred.
Law enforcement sources told TMZ a crime scene was put in place by police when they arrived to the home where Luci4 had died, and his grandparents are now suspicious of his death.
The Los Angeles Fire Department arrived to the home at 11:40AM after receiving a medical call, however the individual had already passed when they arrived and police were contacted, the LAFD told TMZ.
Rapper Luci4 has passed away at age 23
A crime scene was established when police arrived, law enforcement sources told the publication.
An investigation is now underway and it's not yet known if foul play is being considered.
His grandparents have also said Luci4 died on February 22 while spending time at a friend's Los Angeles home. They are suspicious of his death.
They claimed that their grandson's wallet was emptied and that they had recently urged him to be mindful of his circle amid his rising fame.
Now they are awaiting an explanation from police.
Luci4's manager Kayla G revealed the loss with his followers, writing in a statement:  'I am devastated to inform you that today James, Luci4, axxturel has passed away. He was truly a leader. A king. And musician. And a genius.
'There's nobody like him and there will never be. We all loved him dearly. Rest easy.
'Please allow family and friends privacy and patience during this difficult time. Love you.'
A trailblazer in the sigilkore microgenre, Luci4 - born James Dear - is behind the songs BodyPartz, idk anymore, and more
In a statement shared with The Daily Mail, Kayla said of the loss: 'It has definitely been tough for friends and family.'
'I was the second person to find out he passed, I had to break the news to his mother and it was truly devastating. He was a self built artist who was such a kind and selfless person. As his manager and someone very close to him he was so creative and ambitious.
'We had so much love for each other, I was one of the only people in his life aside from a few friends that continued to look after him and gave efforts to make sure he had the right people around him. There will never be another artist who can create a genre (sigilkore) and change the course of music the same way he did.'
She added: 'In regards to his grandparents and the crime scene: I’ve kept in close contact with the family since his passing. His death was sudden and is currently being investigated. We hadn’t received the autopsy but the family and I have our thoughts/concerns but we are awaiting more information patiently so nobody comes to harmful conclusions.'
The Atlantic Records artist, who also goes by Axxturel and 4Jay, is described on his Spotify bio as a 'pioneer of Sigilkore,' a niche genre of trap music dating back to the late 2010s originating from Soundcloud's underground scene.
His signature style is marked by 'dark, brooding lo-fi atmosphere, intricate and disorienting production, and pitched-up vocals layered with various DAW effects and tricks,' according to his bio.
Visually, his art features heavy references to the devil, according to Pitchfork, with the visualizer for BodyPartz featuring a soldier unsuccessfully facing off against a demon.
Luci4's music won over TikTokers, with a few of his songs going viral on the platform - including BodyPartz, which was certified gold by the Recording Industry Association of America in 2024.
